standard.title: Create referenced economic arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge and research findings
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can create descriptions, explanations and arguments using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings at Year 9 level (AC9HE9S05). They have practised using discipline-specific vocabulary, presenting structured arguments and acknowledging sources. Y10 builds on this with more complex arguments, authoritative tone, and use of a broader vocabulary set across the full Year 10 topic scope.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, incorporating and acknowledging research findings for varied purposes and audiences.

nodes.label: Using economic vocabulary accurately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use economic and business terms accurately and contextually — selecting the right term for the right idea and using it in a way that demonstrates understanding.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least five economic or business terms accurately in an explanation of an economic issue, selecting terms that are appropriate to the specific topic.
nodes.typical_width: Use economic and business terms accurately in written and oral communication, including terms such as 'economic indicators', 'government intervention', 'fiscal policy', 'standard of living', 'economic performance', 'federal Budget', 'productivity', 'organisational structures', 'workforce management', 'superannuation', 'interdependence', 'trade', 'comparative advantage', 'globalisation', 'supply chain' and 'insurance'.
wider: Analyse how expert economic commentators (RBA Governor, Treasury Secretary) use technical vocabulary strategically to shape audience understanding and evaluate the communicative choices made
Compare how the same economic concept is described for specialist audiences (academic, policy) vs general audiences (news, social media) and evaluate what is gained and lost
Investigate how economic terminology has evolved — identifying terms that have changed meaning, been replaced or become contested — and evaluate implications for communication
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate vocabulary use is the baseline for credible economic communication. Students who use terms loosely or interchangeably (e.g. confusing 'fiscal' and 'monetary', or 'income' and 'wealth') undermine the authority of their arguments.

response_modes.reason: Practise accurate term use across multiple topics — not just in one explanation. Repeated use in varied contexts builds precision. Peer feedback on vocabulary accuracy is particularly effective here.

success_criteria: Uses at least five economic terms accurately, in context, without significant definitional errors
Selects terms appropriate to the specific topic (i.e. does not apply terms generically across all topics)

nodes.label: Creating descriptions and explanations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create structured descriptions and explanations of economic issues that orient the audience to the issue and incorporate research findings with acknowledgement.
nodes.minimum_width: Write a structured explanation of one economic issue that includes context-setting, key concepts with accurate vocabulary, and at least one acknowledged research finding.
nodes.typical_width: Create descriptions and explanations that orient the audience to the issue using relevant economic concepts and terms; incorporate and acknowledge research findings in appropriate formats such as reports and webpages; explain decisions and conclusions supported by reasons and data representations.
wider: Create an explanation for two different audiences (e.g. peers and business representatives) on the same economic issue and evaluate what changes and why
Write an explanation that incorporates visual data representation (table, chart) and explains how the visual supports the written argument
Investigate the conventions of economic reporting (executive summary, findings, evidence base) and produce an explanation that follows professional conventions

response_modes.reason: Apply explanation writing to varied economic topics and varied audiences — the skill transfers when students have practised it across contexts rather than perfected it for one.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Audience-differentiated explanation writing and integration of data representation into written argument develop genuinely transferable communication capabilities. Professional report conventions add real-world relevance.
success_criteria: Produces an explanation that context-sets the issue before developing the explanation
Incorporates and acknowledges at least one research finding (with attribution)

nodes.label: Constructing economic arguments
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can construct an argument for a course of action in response to an economic or business issue, applying an authoritative tone appropriate to purpose and audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Write one argument for a course of action on an economic issue, including at least one reason supported by evidence and an appropriate concluding recommendation.
nodes.typical_width: Present an argument for a proposal in response to an economic or business issue, applying authoritative tone appropriate to the purpose and audience (e.g. business manager, entrepreneur); support the argument with reasons and data representations; make and justify predictions about impacts.
wider: Construct a counter-argument to a position on an economic issue and evaluate which argument is stronger based on the evidence available
Write an economic policy argument for a government audience, applying the conventions of policy communication (problem statement, evidence base, recommended action, evaluation criteria)
Investigate how persuasive rhetoric and economic evidence interact in political economic communication and evaluate whether the argument is driven by evidence or framing

response_modes.reason: Apply argument construction to varied economic issues and varied audiences — the skill must generalise beyond practice in one context. Different topics require different evidence bases and different argumentative moves.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Counter-argument construction, policy communication conventions and the analysis of rhetoric vs evidence in economic argument develop sophisticated communicative and evaluative capability well beyond the descriptor's minimum.
success_criteria: Presents a clear claim for a course of action at the start of the argument
Supports the claim with at least one piece of evidence and one reason, and uses authoritative rather than tentative tone
